claims.text: FeNiCrMn HEA has excellent corrosion resistance.
Eliminating Co from FeNiCrMn relative to the Cantor alloy provides a cost benefit.
Samples will be examined in as-synthesized or heat-treated states.
The proposed protocol couples digital image correlation with synchrotron X-ray microscopy during mechanical loading.
Coupled in situ testing will reveal real-time deformation and failure mechanisms in FeNiCrMn.
Potential observable mechanisms include dislocation activity, phase transformations, and grain-boundary responses.
These real-time mechanisms are not captured by conventional post-mortem analysis.
Observed deformation mechanisms may correlate with improved mechanical performance under service-like conditions.
Room and moderately elevated temperatures with controlled strain rates can represent service-relevant aerospace, energy, and automotive conditions.
High-resolution in situ imaging can capture dislocation motion, phase transitions, and grain-boundary modifications during deformation.
The in situ approach permits direct observation of the initiation and evolution of slip, twinning, or phase transformation.
Slip, twinning, and phase transformation govern the alloy's strength and ductility.
Linking in situ microstructural changes to load and strain measurements will connect deformation mechanisms with macroscopic mechanical performance.
Distinct events such as dislocation pile-ups or phase changes will correlate with load-induced strain and mechanical response.
Conventional ex situ mechanical evaluation assesses only the final state after deformation.
Synchrotron imaging resolution may constrain which deformation mechanisms can be observed.
The observable response may depend on whether the alloy is as-cast or heat-treated.
Extreme conditions or high strain rates may prevent some mechanisms from being captured in real time.
The magnitude of observable microstructural changes and the contribution of each mechanism to mechanical performance are uncertain and may vary with testing conditions.
